items.text: Under MCL 500.1222(1), which of the following alone is enough to violate the adjuster-license requirement, even without ever touching a claim file?

A. Holding yourself out to the public as an adjuster — MCL 500.1222(1) prohibits adjusting a loss, advertising as an adjuster, or holding oneself out to the public as an adjuster, unless licensed. Holding out alone triggers the prohibition; the other options describe exempt or unrelated roles.

A homeowner in Wayne County is approached by a restoration contractor who offers to 'handle the whole insurance claim' for a fee tied to the settlement amount. Which Michigan statute does this conduct implicate, and is there a contractor exemption?

C. MCL 500.1222; no, there is no contractor exemption among the exactly five exemptions in subsection (2) — MCL 500.1222(2) lists exactly five exemptions (attorney, marine average adjuster, insurer employee, producer with claim authority, supervised data-entry clerk). There is no contractor exemption, so offering to 'handle the claim' for a percentage fee sits inside the prohibited conduct.
Jacob is an officer of a Michigan restoration contracting company and wants to also hold a Michigan adjuster license. What does MCL 500.1224(4) say about this?

C. The commissioner shall not issue the license to anyone connected in any manner with a fire repair contractor — MCL 500.1224(4) categorically bars the commissioner from issuing an adjuster license to a person employed by, owning stock in, an officer or director of, or otherwise connected with a fire repair contractor, regardless of disclosure or ownership percentage.
An adjuster for the insured signs a contract with a homeowner the same day as a kitchen fire. Under MCL 500.1226(4), what right does the homeowner have?

B. The right to void the contract for 10 days after execution, because it was signed within 48 hours of the loss — MCL 500.1226(4): a contract executed within 48 hours after conclusion of the loss-producing occurrence is voidable at the insured's option for 10 days after execution.
An adjuster for the insured charges a client 18% of the insurer's settlement payment on a Michigan property claim. What is the legal problem?

A. The fee exceeds the 10% cap in MCL 500.1226(3) by 8 percentage points — MCL 500.1226(3) caps an adjuster-for-the-insured fee at 10% of the amount paid by the insurer in settlement of the loss. Florida's cap is a different state's statute and does not apply in Michigan.
Which of the following is NOT one of the exactly five exemptions listed in MCL 500.1222(2)?

D. A licensed residential building contractor — The five exemptions are: attorney, marine average adjuster, insurer employee/manager, producer with claim authority, and a supervised data-entry clerk. A licensed residential building contractor is not among them.
In Guldshtadt (DIFS Case No. 25-18350), what fact made the respondent 'connected with' a fire repair contractor?

C. He was listed as CEO on the contractor's California filings and registered agent on its Michigan filings — DIFS found Guldshtadt connected with Evolve Construction & Restoration because he was listed as CEO on its California corporate filings and as its registered agent on its Michigan filings, despite telling an investigator he did not partner with contractors. The categorical licensing bar is MCL 500.1224(4), but the Final Decision's conclusion cited MCL 500.1224(3) and MCL 500.1242(2).
What percentage fee did many of Guldshtadt's unapproved contracts charge, compared to the statutory cap?

D. 35%, more than triple the 10% cap in MCL 500.1226(3) — DIFS's Final Decision found many of Guldshtadt's unapproved contracts contained a 35% fee, more than triple the 10% cap set in MCL 500.1226(3).
Under what statutory authority did DIFS summarily suspend Guldshtadt's adjuster license on November 3, 2025, before any hearing was held?

D. MCL 500.1242(4), the summary-suspension-for-emergency-action authority — The Order for Summary Suspension invokes MCL 24.292(2) of the Administrative Procedures Act and MCL 500.1242(4), which lets the commissioner summarily suspend a license without a prior hearing when emergency action is needed to protect the public.
Was DIFS's Final Decision against Guldshtadt based on a contested hearing where he presented evidence?

B. No, he never requested a hearing, so the unchallenged allegations were accepted as true by default — Guldshtadt never requested a hearing on the summary suspension or the Administrative Complaint despite being given the opportunity and a deadline (March 2, 2026), so DIFS accepted the unchallenged allegations as true under the default procedure.
What is the publication status of Tredenick v Nationwide Agribusiness (Prime Adjusting Service), COA No. 349887, and what does that mean for its precedential weight?

A. Unpublished, per curiam, and therefore persuasive only under MCR 7.215(C)(1) — Tredenick was decided per curiam and is marked UNPUBLISHED. Under MCR 7.215(C)(1), unpublished opinions are persuasive only, not binding precedent, even though the reasoning is grounded in published Supreme Court cases.
In Tredenick, why did the Court of Appeals deny Prime Adjusting Service both its contract fee and a quantum meruit recovery?

D. Because Prime failed to meet the statutory condition precedent of a DIFS-approved contract, so there was no inequity in denying payment — The court held that because Prime failed to meet the MCL 500.1226(4) condition precedent, 'there is no inherit [sic] inequity in denying it payment for those services,' closing off both the contract claim and quantum meruit. The opinion prints 'inherit,' not 'inherent.'
A Michigan attorney negotiates a fire-insurance settlement for a client and charges a contingency fee. Does the attorney need to be licensed as an adjuster or insurance counselor?

A. No, MCL 500.1222(2)(a) and MCL 500.1232 both exempt attorneys admitted to practice law in Michigan — MCL 500.1222(2)(a) exempts attorneys from the adjuster-license requirement, and MCL 500.1232 states it 'does not apply to a person admitted to the practice of law in this state.' The State Bar's own regime governs the attorney's conduct instead.

A contractor's contract calls a percentage-of-recovery fee a 'consulting fee for our experience as contractors.' Under MCL 500.1232, is the word 'consulting' alone always illegal in an insurance context?

A. No, the ban is conditional: it applies only where the term implies the person is a licensed insurance counselor — MCL 500.1232's second sentence bans 'consultant' or 'consulting services' only 'in a way which implies that he or she is a licensed insurance counselor.' It is not an absolute ban on the word; the bigger risk is the section's separate ban on unlicensed advice about a policy's value.
DIFS finds that an adjuster knowingly violated a cease-and-desist order previously issued under MCL 500.1244(1). What is the maximum fine per violation and per order under MCL 500.1244(3)?

C. $20,000 per violation, $100,000 per order — MCL 500.1244(3) sets a higher tier for knowingly violating a cease-and-desist order: up to $20,000 per violation, capped at $100,000 per order, plus suspension or revocation of the license.
Which vendor does DIFS use to administer Michigan's insurance adjuster licensing exams, and what is the flat exam fee?

D. PSI Services LLC, $41 — DIFS contracts with PSI Services LLC (test-takers.psiexams.com/midifs) to administer its insurance licensing exams. The flat examination fee is $41, non-refundable and valid one year from payment.
An applicant files a resident adjuster license application through NIPR but does not pass the PSI exam within the required window. What happens?

C. The applicant must submit a new license application and fee and reschedule the exam, because the application and 6-month window have lapsed — DIFS's licensing page states an application is good for six months from entry into its database, and if the exam is not passed within six months, the applicant must submit a new license application and fee and reschedule the examination.
Does Chapter 12 of the Michigan Insurance Code, or the DIFS adjuster licensing page, impose a continuing-education requirement on licensed adjusters?

B. No CE requirement for adjusters was found in the sections and pages opened; producers have a separate CE requirement under MCL 500.1204c — No continuing-education requirement for adjusters appears in Chapter 12 or on the DIFS licensing page opened this run. Producers, a different license category, have a CE requirement under MCL 500.1204c; that rule does not carry over to adjusters. No bond requirement was found either.
How does Florida's public-adjuster statute, Fla. Stat. 626.854(1), address a person who tries to avoid the definition by describing their claim-handling services differently?

B. It defines a public adjuster as covering such conduct 'regardless of how that person describes or presents his or her services' — Fla. Stat. 626.854(1) defines a public adjuster as anyone who prepares, completes, or files a claim, or negotiates a settlement, for value, 'regardless of how that person describes or presents his or her services,' an explicit anti-relabeling clause. Michigan's MCL 500.1222 has no equivalent sentence.

A licensed contractor in Florida wants to discuss their own repair bid directly with the property owner's insurer. Under Fla. Stat. 626.854(16), what condition keeps this from being unlicensed public adjusting?

D. The discussion must be for the usual and customary fees applicable to the work as stated in the contractor's own contract with the insured — Fla. Stat. 626.854(16) allows a licensed contractor to discuss or explain a construction or repair bid with the insurer or homeowner if doing so for the usual and customary fees applicable to the work to be performed, as stated in the contractor's own contract.
